common_name: Jade Satin Scindapsus (Solid-Green Satin Pothos, Unpatterned Silver Pothos)

planting.note: Root single-node stem cuttings in moist chunky aroid mix or water in spring or early summer, when warmth speeds callusing; 'Jade Satin' shows off its uniform color best under bright indirect light rather than deep shade.

directions: Unlike its heavily silver-patterned relatives 'Argyraeus' and 'Exotica', 'Jade Satin' carries little to no visible variegation, instead prized for its thick, semi-matte, pastel-to-mid-green heart-shaped leaves with a soft satin sheen and a slightly puckered, quilted texture. The near-solid coloring makes it a calmer, more uniform foil for busier variegated houseplants in mixed displays. Grow in bright indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix, letting the top inch dry between waterings; deeper shade dulls the satin sheen and slows growth. Trailing or trained up a moss pole, it climbs and branches modestly, and is commonly (if inaccurately) sold under the same 'Jade Satin' trade name as the unrelated aroid Amydrium medium, so confirm the seller's botanical name before buying.

planting.note: Propagate from single-node stem cuttings in spring or early summer; bright, consistent indirect light through the growing season keeps the heavy silver dappling from reverting toward plain green.

directions: 'Silver Splash' is easily confused with 'Exotica' at a glance, but its variegation reads as a dappled, diffuse silver haze rather than 'Exotica's sharply blocked patches, with the metallic color blending softly into the green background instead of showing a crisp edge. Leaves are thick, quilted, and heart-shaped like other satin pothos forms, with a low-sheen surface that gives the silvering a frosted, almost blue-tinted cast in bright light. Grow in bright indirect light in fast-draining potting mix, allowing the top inch to dry between waterings, and provide a moss pole or trellis if a fuller, more upright climbing habit is wanted; in a hanging basket it trails and branches freely. It is less commonly offered than 'Argyraeus' or 'Exotica', so nursery availability varies by season.

planting.note: Take single-node cuttings that include a stable mint-variegated section and root them against a moss pole in bright indirect light; the pale sectors carry less chlorophyll, so growth is slower than the plain species.

directions: 'Mint' expresses a distinct cool, pale mint-green variegation across its fenestrated leaves — in streaks, sectors, or occasionally whole leaves — that reads noticeably softer and greener than the crisp white-and-green splitting seen on the more widely grown 'Variegata' form of the same species. Give it strong bright indirect light on a moss pole or trellis to support the reduced photosynthetic area in the pale tissue; direct sun can still scorch the lighter sectors even though more light is needed overall than for solid-green Mini Monstera. Let the top inch or two of chunky, well-draining aroid mix dry between waterings. Because variegation stability varies by cutting, buy plants showing variegation low on multiple nodes and prune back fully reverted green growth to preserve the mint pattern.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Rhaphidophora tetrasperma

common_name: Jungle Boogie Philodendron (Tiger Tooth Philodendron, Sawtooth Self-Heading Philodendron)

planting.note: Divide offsets or root basal cuttings in spring in a warm, humid environment; this self-heading hybrid needs no climbing support and matures into a large architectural floor specimen over several years.

directions: This self-heading philodendron hybrid, also traded as 'Henderson's Pride' or the 'Tiger Tooth' philodendron, is grown for its long, narrow, deep-green leaves with dramatically undulating, serrated margins that give each blade a jagged, sawtooth silhouette quite unlike the smooth-edged leaves of most philodendrons. Rather than climbing, it forms an upright, non-vining rosette on a thickening trunk-like base as it matures, making it a bold, sculptural floor or tabletop accent depending on pot size. Grow in bright, indirect light — low light causes leggy, thin growth and less-pronounced serration — in a well-draining, chunky aroid mix, letting the top inch or two dry between waterings. It tolerates average indoor humidity better than many fine-textured aroids but still benefits from occasional misting or a pebble tray in dry rooms.

common_name: Variegated Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron (Variegated Horsehead Philodendron, Variegated Violin Philodendron)

planting.note: Root single-node stem cuttings that include stable variegated tissue in warm, humid conditions with bright indirect light; because this chimeric sport propagates unpredictably from cuttings, growth is slower and pricier than the plain green species.

directions: This chimeric variegated sport of the fiddle-shaped Horsehead Philodendron breaks its elongated, violin-profiled leaves into irregular patches and streaks of creamy white, pale yellow, and green, with the balance shifting unpredictably from leaf to leaf — some nearly half-white, others only lightly marbled. As with other unstable variegates, the white tissue lacks chlorophyll, so plants need consistently bright indirect light to grow well and to keep the pattern from fading back toward solid green, while direct sun can scorch the pale sections. Provide a moss pole or trellis, since leaf size and the distinctive two-lobed fiddle shape develop more fully as the vine climbs than when left to trail. Grow in well-draining, chunky aroid mix and let the top inch dry between waterings; prune any shoots that revert to fully green growth to keep the plant's variegated sectors dominant.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Philodendron bipennifolium species notes
